The Anti-Corn Law League. A mass political movement that defeated one of Britain's most entrenched protectionist policies and revealed the rising power of industrial interests over agricultural privilege.

The Corn Laws had been enacted to protect British grain farmers from foreign competition after the Napoleonic Wars ended. They did their job: they kept bread prices artificially high. But this protection came at the expense of workers and the growing class of industrial manufacturers. Working-class people had demanded repeal since the nineteen twenties. They were starving while grain remained expensive behind protective tariffs.

In 1839, two Manchester merchants, Richard Cobden and John Bright, both radical manufacturers themselves, founded the Anti-Corn Law League. Their argument was elegant: free trade would benefit all classes, lower prices, and increase overall prosperity. It was not just an economic claim but a moral one.

The League organized at a scale never before seen for a political cause. They held mass public meetings across the country. They launched petition drives. Their 1845 petition claimed over three million signatures—a staggering number for the time. They built a sophisticated electoral machine that fielded candidates and organized voters.

The turning point came when Robert Peel, the Prime Minister, experienced a conversion. Peel had started his career as a protectionist, defending the interests of landowners and farmers. But he was convinced by two forces. First, the economic arguments for free trade were persuasive. Second, and more urgently, the Irish Famine of 1845 and 1846 forced him to confront the human cost of policies that kept food expensive. In 1846, he brought the repeal of the Corn Laws to Parliament.

His decision shattered the Conservative Party. Protectionist Tories, led by Benjamin Disraeli, denounced Peel as a traitor to his class and his party. The split was so severe that it left the Liberal Party dominant for decades. Free trade had won, and the industrial class that had pushed for it had seized power from the old agricultural elite.

The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 opened an era of British free trade and commercial expansion. Britain's industrial power would grow under this system, and the country would cement its position as a global economic and imperial power. The victory belonged to Cobden and Bright, to the merchants of Manchester, and to the ordinary working people whose hunger had driven the demand for change.
